prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of flat bands in twisted bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states at the magic angle, opening the field of moire quantum materials

statement.case_for: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene is the case I can support most firmly on the shortlist beyond my own opening first choice (B037, which no colleague ranked). It rests on a simple, general mechanism: two lattices with a small relative twist produce a moire pattern and, at a particular angle, nearly flat bands in the Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model. That is the kind of clean, analysable model that explains a messy many-body phenomenon, and it made a quantitative prediction that experiment then tested. The 2018 observation of correlated insulators and superconductivity by Jarillo-Herrero's group turned the prediction into a platform that many groups have reproduced, and it has since generalised to twisted TMDs and fractional Chern insulators. It has the broadest opening support of any candidate except optical clocks (six of eight members ranked it, three in their top three, including the first choice of Olle Eriksson), and theory and experiment are tightly linked, which gives a natural three-person allocation of prediction (Bistritzer, MacDonald) and discovery (Jarillo-Herrero).
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is maturity: the discovery is about eight years old and the pairing mechanism of the superconductivity, and the nature of several correlated states, remain unsettled, so one could say we reward a platform before we understand it. Attribution is also open: Yuan Cao, first author of the 2018 experiments, other early moire work (Dean, Kim, and the earlier twist-angle theory of Lopes dos Santos and collaborators) and independent confirmations are not captured by a three-name limit. Optical lattice clocks (B042) have a cleaner two-person attribution and a more settled interpretation, so a reasonable member could prefer to reward the mature case first.

responses.point: Danielsson ranked twisted bilayer graphene only seventh and flagged that the origin of the superconductivity is unresolved and that credit within the experimental team is not settled, so timing is somewhat early.
responses.response: I accept the point that the pairing mechanism is open, and I would not let the citation claim an explanation of it. But the prize is for the discovery of the phases and of the flat-band mechanism that predicted where to look, and both are independently reproduced by many groups with stable single-particle theory. We have rewarded phenomena before their microscopic origin was settled when the phenomenon itself was robust. I agree that credit within the experimental team is a real difficulty, and I would rather say so openly in the citation wording than hide it. I do not, however, think that difficulty is worse than for his own first choice, where three individuals stand in for collaborations of thousands.

responses.point: Eriksson ranked it first as a clean case of theory anticipating a new state of matter, with a natural prediction-versus-discovery split among Bistritzer, MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero, while noting the first author and other twist-angle theorists are not credited.
responses.response: I largely agree and share the reading that the Bistritzer-MacDonald model is the central scientific idea. I would push on one point, though: the prediction that mattered was the continuum-model estimate of the magic angle with the flat bands, and the earlier numerical twist-angle work by Lopes dos Santos and collaborators is a genuine priority question that we should not wave away. Whether it displaces a name, or only shapes the citation, is something I cannot settle from the files. I also think the correlated-state mechanism is a bigger open issue than he suggests, so I prefer a narrow citation.

responses.point: Olsson ranked it second, calling allocation among the three names fairly clean, but noted that the first author Yuan Cao and other groups (Dean, Young, Efetov, Ashoori) made major early contributions and that the superconducting mechanism is unresolved.
responses.response: I agree on the strength of the experimental core and on the credit problem, and I would go slightly further: the claim that allocation is fairly clean holds for the senior-author logic, but not for the scientific one, since the student-led measurements and the hBN-moire work by Dean and Kim are real contributions. I think the three-person rule forces us to credit the conceptual origin (theory) and the leader of the decisive experiment, and I would defend that as the standard we have used for large experimental teams. Her preference for B028 is a different kind of case, an instrument invention, and I do not think its maturity advantage outweighs the weaker discovery content.

responses.point: Lindroth ranked optical lattice clocks first, arguing that Katori's magic-wavelength insight is a clean, well-understood use of atomic physics with a clear conceptual origin, a natural two-person split and a non-controversial, timely field.
responses.response: I agree that B042 has the cleanest attribution of anything on the list and the strongest independent confirmation, and I ranked it seventh mainly because my own judgement of precision metrology is limited, not because I doubt it. Where I differ is on novelty: frequency combs (2005) and ion clocks (2012) already sit next to it, so I read the lattice clock more as a decisive performance advance than as a new regime of physics, whereas moire flat bands are a new mechanism. I would therefore keep B042 as my first alternative and would not object strongly if the committee preferred it on maturity grounds.

uncertainties: Whether twist-angle theory predating Bistritzer-MacDonald (Lopes dos Santos and collaborators) should alter the credited theory names; I cannot verify this from the provided material.
Whether recognition of Yuan Cao and the broader experimental teams can be handled through the citation wording alone.
Whether the committee will accept that the superconducting pairing mechanism is not needed for the discovery to be prize-worthy.
Whether a KPZ prize (B037) could be made attributionally fair without the exact-solution contributors, and whether any colleague finds it competitive.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the credited candidates. I know of no collaboration or institutional tie to MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero, Bistritzer or the other shortlisted names. I share the Gothenburg physics environment with Johansson and Olsson, but neither is a credited candidate here.
